1.q: שְׁלֹמֹ֨ה בְנִ֥⁠י אֶחָ֛ד בָּֽחַר־בּ֥⁠וֹ אֱלֹהִ֖ים נַ֣עַר וָ⁠רָ֑ךְ
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that **God has chosen** Solomon first in this sentence. Alternate translation: [God has chosen my son Solomon alone, but he is young and tender]
See how you translated the same expression in 22:5. Alternate translation: [and lacks experience]

1.q: וְ⁠הַ⁠מְּלָאכָ֣ה גְדוֹלָ֔ה כִּ֣י לֹ֤א לְ⁠אָדָם֙ הַ⁠בִּירָ֔ה כִּ֖י לַ⁠יהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהִֽים
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and since the temple is not for man but for Yahweh God, the work is great]

2.note: Here and in many similar contexts throughout this chapter, the term **house** means “temple.” Alternate translation: [for the temple of my God]

David is using the adjective **gold** as a noun to mean a certain kind of item or article, one made from gold. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. You can do the same with the terms **silver**, **bronze**, **iron**, and **wood** in this verse and with the similar expressions in verse 5. Alternate translation: [gold for the golden items]

The words **onyx** and **settings** together express a single idea. The word **onyx** tells what kind of **settings** these are. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [stones of onyx for settings]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **variegation**, you could express the same idea in another way. The UST models one way to do that.
David is saying **every** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. The UST models one way to do that.

4.q: שְׁלֹ֧שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֛ים כִּכְּרֵ֥י זָהָ֖ב & וְ⁠שִׁבְעַ֨ת אֲלָפִ֤ים כִּכַּר־כֶּ֨סֶף֙ מְזֻקָּ֔ק
4.note: See how you decided to represent the value or weight of a “kikkar” in 20:2 and follow the same approach here and in verse 7.
See how you translated the term “houses in 28:11. Alternate translation: [the buildings]

5.note: Here, **hand** represents the activity of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that the craftsmen will do]

5.q: וּ⁠מִ֣י מִתְנַדֵּ֔ב לְ⁠מַלֹּ֥אות יָד֛⁠וֹ הַ⁠יּ֖וֹם לַ⁠יהוָֽה
5.note: David is using the question form to challenge these Israelite leaders to contribute generously to the temple, as he has done. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I hope that many of you will fill your hands today to Yahweh]

David is using **to fill his hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to bring a gift” or “to make a donation.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to bring a gift] or [to make a donation]

6.q: וַ⁠יִּֽתְנַדְּבוּ֩ שָׂרֵ֨י הָ⁠אָב֜וֹת וְ⁠שָׂרֵ֣י ׀ שִׁבְטֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וְ⁠שָׂרֵ֤י הָ⁠אֲלָפִים֙ וְ⁠הַ⁠מֵּא֔וֹת וּ⁠לְ⁠שָׂרֵ֖י מְלֶ֥אכֶת הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
6.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put all the information together about who **offered** further gifts for the temple. Alternate translation: [Then the leaders of the fathers, the leaders of the tribes of Israel, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and the commanders of the work of the king offered freely]
See how you translated the similar expression “heads of fathers” in 9:9. Alternate translation: [the leaders of fathers’ houses]

7.note: Since the author uses the specific number **10,000** later in the verse, it is possible that he is using the term **myriad**, which also means 10,000, as a round, symbolic number to represent a very large, uncountable number. Your language may have a number of its own that it uses with that meaning. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [and more darics than anyone could count] or [and a very large number of darics]

The term **darics** describes the standard gold coins of the Persian era, the time when the author wrote this book. A daric contained about 8 or 9 grams of gold. Those coins did not exist at the time of the events the author is describing, but he is using a term that his readers will recognize in order to help them appreciate what happened. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [gold coins]

8.note: The author is using **being found with it** as a common expression of his culture to mean “who had it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the ones who had precious stones gave them] or [And the owners of precious stones gave them]

Here, **hand** represents the control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the custody of Jehiel the Gershonite]

9.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because the people had offered freely, they rejoiced]
Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an elaboration. Alternate translation: [and they had done that because]
Here the **heart** represents a person’s feelings and commitments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with complete devotion]

9.q: וְ⁠גַם֙ דָּוִ֣יד הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ שָׂמַ֖ח שִׂמְחָ֥ה גְדוֹלָֽה
9.note: The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And King David also rejoiced very greatly]

10.note: The author is using the term **eyes** to represent “sight.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the sight of all of the assembly] or [as all of the assembly watched]

The expression **Blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. See how you translated the similar expression in 16:36. Alternate translation: [May people bless you] or [We bless you]
David is using the term **father** to mean “ancestor.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our ancestor]

11.q: לְ⁠ךָ֣ יְ֠הוָה הַ⁠גְּדֻלָּ֨ה וְ⁠הַ⁠גְּבוּרָ֤ה וְ⁠הַ⁠תִּפְאֶ֨רֶת֙ וְ⁠הַ⁠נֵּ֣צַח וְ⁠הַ⁠ה֔וֹד כִּי־כֹ֖ל בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֣יִם וּ⁠בָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ לְ⁠ךָ֤
11.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since everything in the heavens and on the earth is to you, to you, Yahweh, are greatness and might and glory and splendor and majesty]

The terms **greatness** and **might** mean similar things. So do the terms **glory** and **splendor**. In each case, David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [huge power and great glory]
See how you translated the similar expression in 16:31. Alternate translation: [throughout all of creation]

David is using Yahweh **lifting** himself **above all** to represent Yahweh taking authority over everything. He is using the term **head** to mean “ruler.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state these meanings plainly. Alternate translation: [The kingdom belongs to you, since you have taken authority over everything as ruler]

12.note: David is using Yahweh’s **face** to represent his “presence.” He is referring to the way a king would summon someone into his presence in order to confer some honor on him or give him something valuable. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And wealth and glory come from you]

In this instance, **hand** represents a person possessing something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you possess power and might]

The terms **power** and **might** mean similar things. Speaker is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [very great power]

In this instance, **hand** represents the capability of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have the capability to exalt and to strengthen all]

13.note: See how you translated this expression in 17:7.

David is using the possessive form to describe a **name** that is characterized by **glory**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your glorious name]

David is using the term **name** to represent Yahweh’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you for your glorious reputation] or [you for your glorious qualities and deeds]

14.q: וְ⁠כִ֨י מִ֤י אֲנִי֙ וּ⁠מִ֣י עַמִּ֔⁠י כִּֽי־נַעְצֹ֣ר כֹּ֔חַ לְ⁠הִתְנַדֵּ֖ב כָּ⁠זֹ֑את
14.note: David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But I and my people do not really have the power to offer freely like this.]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [After all,]

Here, **hand** represents a person possessing something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and what we have given to you already belonged to you]

15.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an elaboration. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

David is using the expression **to your face ** to mean “in your presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are foreigners and settlers in your presence]

The terms **foreigners** and **settlers** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. They both referred to people from another country who were living in a land without the right to own property there. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [we are landless immigrants to your face]

David is speaking as if the Israelites were actually **foreigners** and **settlers** in their own land and as if Yahweh were a native of the land, in whose presence they were living. He means that it is as if they do not have any means of production, while Yahweh does. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everything we have comes from you; we are not able to produce anything ourselves]

David is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 18. Alternate translation: [and the same was true of all of our ancestors]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **shadow** is fleeting, so are the **days** of a person’s life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. The UST models one way to do that.

David does not mean that every person’s life is completely **without hope**. He means specifically that no person has the hope of continuing to live and never dying. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and without hope of not dying]

16.note: See how you translated the similar expression “the name of your glory” in 29:13. Alternate translation: [for your holy name] or [for your holy reputation]
See how you translated the expression “from your hand” in 29:14. Alternate translation: [it already belongs to you]

17.note: Here the **heart** represents a person’s motives and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each person’s motives]

David is using the plural **uprightnesses** where he could have used the singular form. This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the sincere quality of this attribute. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and are pleased with genuine uprightness]

The expression **are pleased** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and that genuine uprightness pleases you]
David is continuing to use the **heart** to represent a person’s motives and intentions. Alternate translation: [With genuinely upright intentions]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I have offered** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his personal role in the activity he describes so that he can then refer to the complementary role of the **people**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For my part, I have offered freely]

David is using the demonstrative adjective **these** as a noun to mean the gifts he has given. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [all of these gifts]

17.q: וְ⁠עַתָּ֗ה עַמְּ⁠ךָ֙ הַ⁠נִּמְצְאוּ־פֹ֔ה רָאִ֥יתִי בְ⁠שִׂמְחָ֖ה לְ⁠הִֽתְנַדֶּב־לָֽ⁠ךְ
17.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put David’s observation that he sees **with rejoicing** at the start of this sentence. Alternate translation: [And now I see with rejoicing that your people found here have offered freely to you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 24:4. Alternate translation: [your people who are here]

18.q: שֳׁמְרָ⁠ה־זֹּ֣את לְ⁠עוֹלָ֔ם לְ⁠יֵ֥צֶר מַחְשְׁב֖וֹת לְבַ֣ב עַמֶּ֑⁠ךָ
18.note: Since, in this context, the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts, it might seem that also saying **intention** and **thoughts** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can shorten this expression. Alternate translation: [make this something that your people forever intend]

In this instance, the **heart** represents a person’s feelings and commitments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and establish their loyalty toward you] or [and establish them as loyal toward you]

19.note: David is once again using the **heart** to represent a person’s feelings and commitments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a sincere commitment]

The terms **commandments**, **testimonies**, and **statutes** mean similar things. David is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [to obey all of your laws]

The phrases **to do everything** and **to build** together express a single idea. The phrase **do everything** tells in what way Solomon would **build** the temple. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. The UST models one way to do that.

21.note: The author is using **the morrow of that day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “the following morning.” He does not mean the morning of the same day when David addressed the assembly. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the following morning] or [on the morning of the next day]

22.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [for time number two]

The author is using the adjective **second** as a noun to mean a certain thing, a time or occasion. (He is referring back to [23:1](ta:23), when David first “made Solomon his son reign.”) The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **time**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [as they had done once before]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **a leader**, he means Solomon, not some other person. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they anointed him as a leader for Yahweh] or [and they anointed him as king of Yahweh’s people]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they anointed Zadok to be the high priest]

23.note: The author assumes that his readers will know that by **listened**, he means that the Israelites did what Solomon told them to do. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and all of the Israelites obeyed him]

24.q: וְ⁠כָל־הַ⁠שָּׂרִים֙ וְ⁠הַ⁠גִּבֹּרִ֔ים וְ⁠גַ֕ם כָּל־בְּנֵ֖י הַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ דָּוִ֑יד נָ֣תְנוּ יָ֔ד תַּ֖חַת שְׁלֹמֹ֥ה הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
24.note: The author is speaking as if these leaders had actually held Solomon up with their hands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all of the leaders and the warriors and also all of the sons of King David supported King Solomon] or [And all of the leaders and the warriors and also all of the sons of King David were loyal to King Solomon]

25.note: See how you translated the expression “to above” in 22:5. Alternate translation: [very great]

The author is using the term **eyes** to mean “perspective,” “judgment,” or “opinion.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the regard of all the Israelites]

The author is speaking as if the **majesty of a kingdom** were a garment that Yahweh could have **put on** Solomon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he made him a majestic king over Israel]

The author is using the expression **to the face of** to mean “before” or “previous to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [such as no king before him had ever had]

27.q: וְ⁠הַ⁠יָּמִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר מָלַךְ֙ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אַרְבָּעִ֖ים שָׁנָ֑ה
27.note: The author is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the time of David’s reign. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the time that he reigned over Israel was 40 years]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [for 33 years]

28.note: The phrases **in good old age** and **full of days** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [when he was quite elderly]

The author assumes that readers will understand that he is using the term **good** to mean “considerable.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [when he was considerably old]

The author is speaking as if **days**, **wealth**, and **glory** were objects and as if David had been a container that was **full** of them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [having lived for many days and obtained much wealth and glory] or [having lived for a long time and obtained much wealth and glory]

29.q: וְ⁠דִבְרֵי֙ דָּוִ֣יד הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ הָ⁠רִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְ⁠הָ⁠אֲחרֹנִ֑ים הִנָּ֣⁠ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ שְׁמוּאֵ֣ל הָ⁠רֹאֶ֔ה וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ נָתָ֣ן הַ⁠נָּבִ֔יא וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵ֖י גָּ֥ד הַ⁠חֹזֶֽה
29.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is using phrases that he will use regularly in 2 Chronicles, as he continues this story of Israel’s kings, to conclude the account of kings’ reigns. If you have already translated the books of 1 Kings and 2 Kings, see how you translated the similar conclusions to accounts of kings’ reigns. Alternate translation: [Now you can read about the matters of King David, the first and the last, in the records that Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet, and Gad the visionary kept]

The author is referring to all of the **matters of King David** (that is, the events of his reign) by naming two extremes, **the first** events and **the last** events. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [events from his entire reign]

29.q: הִנָּ֣⁠ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ שְׁמוּאֵ֣ל הָ⁠רֹאֶ֔ה וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ נָתָ֣ן הַ⁠נָּבִ֔יא וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵ֖י גָּ֥ד הַ⁠חֹזֶֽה
29.note: The author is using the term **words** to represent what these prophets recorded by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [behold them, written in the records of Samuel the seer and in the records of Nathan the prophet and in the records of Gad the visionary]

29.q: הִנָּ֣⁠ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ שְׁמוּאֵ֣ל הָ⁠רֹאֶ֔ה וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ נָתָ֣ן הַ⁠נָּבִ֔יא וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵ֖י גָּ֥ד הַ⁠חֹזֶֽה
29.note: The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [behold Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet, and the visionary have written about them in their records]

30.note: The author does not mean that the things he lists in this verse are in the records of the prophets in addition to the “matters of King David.” He means that these are some of the things that those records contain. If this would not be clear from the word **with**, you may want to use a different connecting word. Alternate translation: [including]

The words **reign** and **might** together express a single idea. The word **might** tells what characterized David’s **reign**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [the many ways in which he reigned mightily]

30.q: וְ⁠הָ⁠עִתִּ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר עָבְר֤וּ עָלָי⁠ו֙ וְ⁠עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠עַ֖ל כָּל־מַמְלְכ֥וֹת הָ⁠אֲרָצֽוֹת
30.note: The author is using **the times that passed over** as a common expression of his culture to mean “the things that happened.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the events that involved him and the Israelites and the foreign kingdoms around them] or [and the things that happened to him and to Israel and to all of the kingdoms of the lands]
